title: AutoIndex: Learning Representation Programs for Retrieval
hook: Stop tuning the retriever — tune the documents. AutoIndex searches for executable programs that rewrite and reorganize docs before indexing, lifting recall on every task with BM25 left untouched.
key_points: Learns 'representation programs' — executable transforms that slice, enrich, normalize, or reorganize documents before indexing.
Treats document representation as an explicit optimization target, not a fixed preprocessing choice made before retrieval.
Validation-guided search: agents diagnose the current program's retrieval failures and synthesize candidate updates, keeping only ones that help.
BM25 is held fixed across all experiments — the gains come purely from changing how documents are represented, not the retriever.
On the CRUMB benchmark, improves recall on all 8 tasks: avg +8.4% Recall@100 and +8.3% nDCG@10, up to +30.5% and +43.6%.
content_html: Most retrieval work tunes the retriever, the reranker, or a handful of preprocessing knobs. AutoIndex flips the target: it searches over representation programs — executable transformations that rewrite raw documents into the form a retriever finally sees — and optimizes those instead, holding a plain BM25 index fixed the whole time.
extra_html:
How it works

A representation program can slice, enrich, normalize, reweight, or reorganize documents before they're indexed. AutoIndex improves it through validation-guided program search: at each iteration, agents diagnose where the current program's retrieval is failing and synthesize candidate updates, keeping only the changes that measurably raise retrieval quality under the resulting index. Because BM25 stays fixed, every gain is attributable to how the documents were represented, not to a better retriever.

Why it matters

Evaluated on CRUMB, a benchmark of heterogeneous retrieval tasks, the learned programs beat a static full-document BM25 baseline on all 8 tasks — average gains of +8.4% Recall@100 and +8.3% nDCG@10, and as much as +30.5% and +43.6% on the hardest. The authors' broader claim is that document representation shouldn't be a fixed choice you make once before retrieval begins, but an explicit thing to optimize. Sam O'Nuallain and colleagues, arXiv 2026; code is released.

related.title: Why RAG? Grounding LLMs in Your Data
related.hook: An LLM only knows what it was trained on — until it's stale, private, or just wrong. RAG bolts on a search step so the model answers from your data and can cite it.

related.title: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)
related.hook: Keyword search misses answers that use different words. DPR embeds questions and passages into one vector space and retrieves by meaning — the backbone of modern vector search.

related.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
related.hook: Why force a model to memorize everything? RAG lets it look things up — fetch relevant documents, then answer from that evidence instead of frozen weights alone.

flashcards.prompt: What does AutoIndex optimize instead of the retriever or reranker?
flashcards.back_html: Representation programs — executable transformations that rewrite documents (slice, enrich, normalize, reorganize) before indexing, while the retriever (BM25) stays fixed.

flashcards.prompt: Why does AutoIndex hold BM25 fixed across all experiments?

choices.text: So any improvement is attributable to how documents are represented, not to a stronger retriever
Because BM25 is the only retriever the framework can search over
Because dense retrievers were too slow to index the corpus

flashcards.explanation_html: With the retriever fixed, the gains isolate the effect of the learned document representation rather than a better matching model.

flashcards.prompt: How does AutoIndex decide which changes to a representation program to keep?
flashcards.back_html: Validation-guided search: agents diagnose the current program's retrieval failures and propose updates, and it retains only those that measurably improve retrieval quality.
